entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion: Not proved.** The evidence gathered so far does not favor Thomas Flynn over Michael Flynn, or either over a third man. No father is concluded and nothing is written to the tree.

### The subject is identified; his childhood household is not
The subject is firmly identified at death. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026, records his death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. It is an original record with primary information about the death, from the attending physician. Its father field is blank; the informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported the father as unknown. That is negative evidence from a secondary informant who was not in a position to know. It names no father, and it is not evidence against any candidate.

The 1860 census places Patrick as a boarder and coal laborer, age 15, in the Owen Donnelly household: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. It is an original record. The residence is primary information. No Flynn adult lives with him, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears as a near neighbor. The record fits a boy born about 1845 but links him to no parent.

### Two equally plausible childhood households in 1850
Two 1850 census entries fit the subject.

- 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 5 (born about 1845), Irish-born.
- 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 6 (born about 1844), Irish-born, in a different enumeration district.

Both are original records. The 1850 census does not state relationships, so each parent-child tie is inferred from household position (indirect evidence). The informant in each is unknown. The ages differ by one year, well within normal census age error for a subject born about 1845, so age cannot choose between them. Both boys are Irish-born, and both households are in Schuylkill County, so place cannot choose either.

### Why the elimination fails
No record bridges 1850 to the adult subject.
1. Neither 1850 entry is tied to the adult Patrick. The only 1860 and 1908 records name no parent and do not connect to either household.
2. Each candidate rests on the untested assumption that the boy in that household is the subject. Both cannot be, and it is possible neither is.
3. The direct evidence a baptism would give was sought in FamilySearch and NLI Catholic parish registers (Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850). No baptism naming a father was found.

The two hypotheses, Thomas as father and Michael as father, each stand on one inferred household entry and nothing else. Neither has contradicting evidence, and neither has corroboration. No conflict is registered. This is two unseparated candidates, and the evidence does not choose between them.

### What is not yet examined
The evidence gathered so far does not settle the question. Records that could still narrow it include:
- a marriage record for Patrick Flynn, which may name his parents;
- the 1870 and 1880 censuses, which may show him living near or with a candidate's family;
- his 1908 obituary and burial record;
- birth, marriage or death records of his children, which may name his father;
- county estate, church or naturalization records for Thomas and Michael Flynn naming sons.

These are reachable record types and have not been searched. Until they are, the question remains open at not proved.

### Tier
Not proved. Two candidates, indirect evidence only, no direct record, and unsearched record types remain. Proofs are never final, and new records could change this.

## Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion: Not proved.** The evidence gathered so far does not favor Thomas Flynn over Michael Flynn, or either over a third man. No father is concluded and nothing is written to the tree.

### The subject is identified; his childhood household is not
The subject is firmly identified at death. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026, records his death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. It is an original record with primary information about the death, from the attending physician. Its father field is blank; the informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported the father as unknown. That is negative evidence from a secondary informant who was not in a position to know. It names no father, and it is not evidence against any candidate.

The 1860 census places Patrick as a boarder and coal laborer, age 15, in the Owen Donnelly household: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. It is an original record. The residence is primary information. No Flynn adult lives with him, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears as a near neighbor. The record fits a boy born about 1845 but links him to no parent.

### Two equally plausible childhood households in 1850
Two 1850 census entries fit the subject.

- 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 5 (born about 1845), Irish-born.
- 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 6 (born about 1844), Irish-born, in a different enumeration district.

Both are original records. The 1850 census does not state relationships, so each parent-child tie is inferred from household position (indirect evidence). The informant in each is unknown. The ages differ by one year, well within normal census age error for a subject born about 1845, so age cannot choose between them. Both boys are Irish-born, and both households are in Schuylkill County, so place cannot choose either.

### Why the elimination fails
No record bridges 1850 to the adult subject.
1. Neither 1850 entry is tied to the adult Patrick. The only 1860 and 1908 records name no parent and do not connect to either household.
2. Each candidate rests on the untested assumption that the boy in that household is the subject. Both cannot be, and it is possible neither is.
3. The direct evidence a baptism would give was sought in FamilySearch and NLI Catholic parish registers (Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850). No baptism naming a father was found.

The two hypotheses, Thomas as father and Michael as father, each stand on one inferred household entry and nothing else. Neither has contradicting evidence, and neither has corroboration. No conflict is registered. This is two unseparated candidates, and the evidence does not choose between them.

### What is not yet examined
The evidence gathered so far does not settle the question. Records that could still narrow it include:
- a marriage record for Patrick Flynn, which may name his parents;
- the 1870 and 1880 censuses, which may show him living near or with a candidate's family;
- his 1908 obituary and burial record;
- birth, marriage or death records of his children, which may name his father;
- county estate, church or naturalization records for Thomas and Michael Flynn naming sons.

These are reachable record types and have not been searched. Until they are, the question remains open at not proved.

### Tier
Not proved. Two candidates, indirect evidence only, no direct record, and unsearched record types remain. Proofs are never final, and new records could change this.

**Conclusion (possible, not yet established):** Thomas Flynn is a credible candidate for Patrick Flynn's father. The evidence is a single indirect record and does not support a firmer finding. No mother has been identified.

### The evidence

The only record gathered is the 1850 U.S. census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, dwelling 84, family 91, the Thomas Flynn household. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. The source is an original record. The household includes a child, Patrick, about age 5, matching Patrick Flynn's expected birth around 1845 (persona linked to the subject at "confident" level).

**Classification.** The 1850 census does not state relationships. The parent-child link is therefore inferred by the researcher from household position and shared surname: the information quality is indeterminate, the informant is unknown (probably Thomas Flynn himself, reporting to the enumerator), and the record basis is inferred. This is indirect evidence. Thomas Flynn's name and headship (about 32 in 1850, so born about 1818, an age consistent with fatherhood) were linked to him at "probable" confidence.

### Why this is not firmer

A same-surname child in a household could be a son, but also a nephew, grandchild, younger relative or unrelated boarder. One co-residence cannot separate these alternatives. No second source corroborates it, and nothing contradicts it. The link between Patrick and Thomas was held by the researcher at "speculative" confidence. The working hypothesis (Thomas Flynn as father) rests on this one line of evidence.

### Tree note

The tree's existing birth fact for Patrick (F1, Birth, about 1845, place given as Ireland, citing S1, the 1850 census) places his birth in Ireland, while the project objective and the research question describe him as born in Pennsylvania. An 1850 census entry would carry a birthplace only if the enumerator recorded one, and the project holds no assertion for it. This discrepancy is not registered as a conflict and does not bear on the household identification here, but it should be checked against the census image and later records because a foreign birthplace would change the likely family context.

### What would resolve it

The 1860 census would show whether Patrick remains with Thomas Flynn and whether a wife of suitable age is present. Patrick's 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate may name both parents directly. Later censuses (1870, 1880) state relationships explicitly. Baptism records and Thomas Flynn's naturalization, will, estate or burial records could independently establish the relationship. Until at least one of these is examined, the parentage is only a possible answer.

Because the parentage stays below the probable threshold, no ParentChild relationship has been written to the tree. This finding may be revised as new evidence appears.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants would outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. That weighing has not been done: c_001 is unresolved, no preferred assertion is recorded, and this conclusion adopts no birthplace.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845-1908): not proved, identity across sources unsettled

**Question.** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, born about 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania?

**Finding.** Identity across the cited sources is not established, so the sources cannot yet be correlated into a parentage conclusion. The candidate father is Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, but no tier above not proved is supported at present. An earlier draft of this summary rated the answer probable; that rating is withdrawn because it correlated sources whose identity to one another is unsettled.

**The evidence.** The 1850 census (dwelling 84, family 91; NARA M432, roll 810) and the 1860 census (dwelling 112, family 119; NARA M653, roll 1141) list a Patrick Flynn, age 5 and then 15, in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County, both recording Ireland as his birthplace. Neither census states relationships, so each is indirect evidence inferred from household position and shared surname. The 1908 death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names Thomas Flynn as father, but its informant was son-in-law James Brown, a secondary informant not present at the birth, and it gives Pennsylvania as Patrick's birthplace.

**The conflict.** Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in both censuses versus Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is unresolved, with no weighing or preferred assertion recorded. Birthplace is an identifying attribute: it bears on whether the census boy and the man who died in 1908 are the same Patrick Flynn. The death certificate's father entry is the only direct statement of parentage, and it rests on the very record whose identity link is in question. Until the conflict is resolved, the census household and the death certificate cannot validly be treated as one person, and no birthplace is adopted.

**What would settle it.** Conflict-resolution should weigh c_001, aided by unsearched records: the 1880 census (relationship column, birthplace of Patrick and of his parents), the 1870 and 1900 censuses, a baptism record, Thomas Flynn's probate, and naturalization or other records of Patrick. These are unsearched record types that could still establish the answer.

**Tier: not proved** (shortfall: conflict). The tree relationship previously written from the earlier probable rating has been removed.

Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants would outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. That weighing has not been done: c_001 is unresolved, no preferred assertion is recorded, and this conclusion adopts no birthplace.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.

**Question.** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, born about 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania?

**Finding.** Identity across the cited sources is not established, so the sources cannot yet be correlated into a parentage conclusion. The candidate father is Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, but no tier above not proved is supported at present. An earlier draft of this summary rated the answer probable; that rating is withdrawn because it correlated sources whose identity to one another is unsettled.

**The evidence.** The 1850 census (dwelling 84, family 91; NARA M432, roll 810) and the 1860 census (dwelling 112, family 119; NARA M653, roll 1141) list a Patrick Flynn, age 5 and then 15, in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County, both recording Ireland as his birthplace. Neither census states relationships, so each is indirect evidence inferred from household position and shared surname. The 1908 death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names Thomas Flynn as father, but its informant was son-in-law James Brown, a secondary informant not present at the birth, and it gives Pennsylvania as Patrick's birthplace.

**The conflict.** Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in both censuses versus Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is unresolved, with no weighing or preferred assertion recorded. Birthplace is an identifying attribute: it bears on whether the census boy and the man who died in 1908 are the same Patrick Flynn. The death certificate's father entry is the only direct statement of parentage, and it rests on the very record whose identity link is in question. Until the conflict is resolved, the census household and the death certificate cannot validly be treated as one person, and no birthplace is adopted.

**What would settle it.** Conflict-resolution should weigh c_001, aided by unsearched records: the 1880 census (relationship column, birthplace of Patrick and of his parents), the 1870 and 1900 censuses, a baptism record, Thomas Flynn's probate, and naturalization or other records of Patrick. These are unsearched record types that could still establish the answer.

# Birthplace of Iram F. Hyde (c. 1796-1799, d. after 1870)

**Conclusion (probable):** Iram Hyde of Jackson, Washington County, New York, and later White County, Indiana, was born in **New Hampshire** about 1796-1798.

## The evidence and the conflict

| Record | Where | Birthplace given | Informant |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1850 US census | Jackson, Washington Co., NY | New Hampshire | Iram's household |
| 1855 NY census (image) | Jackson | **Washington [Co., NY]**; 57 years in town | Iram's household |
| 1860 US census | Jackson | N. Hampshire | Iram's household |
| 1870 US census | West Point Twp., White Co., IN | New Hampshire | daughter Christina Wilson's household |
| 1880 US census (image), daughter Margaret Clark | Mina, Chautauqua Co., NY | father born N Hamshire | daughter Margaret's household |

Sources (FamilySearch): 1850 1:1:MZM9-GG4; 1855 1:1:K63S-P69, image 3:1:33SQ-GBP2-Q28 (image 11, 18 June 1855); 1860 1:1:MCQZ-FKJ; 1870 1:1:MX6L-K5Z; 1880 1:1:MZZC-8WS, image 3:1:33SQ-GYBN-98K4 (p. 10, line 46). The 1855 birthplace and the 1880 parent-birthplace columns are not indexed and were read from the images. All are secondary information.

This is the reported conflict: the federal censuses say New Hampshire; the 1855 New York state census says Washington County, New York.

## Resolution (conflict c_001)

1. **Independence.** 1850, 1855 and 1860 come from Iram's own household. Two independent informants outside it, Christina's household in Indiana (1870) and daughter Margaret in Chautauqua County (1880, after Iram's death), both say New Hampshire.
2. **Quality of the 1855 entry.** Years-resident equals age for Iram (57), Mary (58) and neighbours, a default lifelong pattern; Mary, herself Washington Co.-born, may have answered for both.
3. **Negative evidence.** No Hyde head of household appears in Cambridge (Jackson's parent town until 1815) or Jackson in the 1790-1820 censuses, contradicting lifelong residence from c.1798.

New Hampshire is preferred on the preponderance of evidence. A birth elsewhere in Washington County cannot be fully excluded.

## Identity

Rare given name, consistent age, wife Mary (Robertson), Jackson residence 1826-1860 (land records 3:1:3QSQ-G9WC-F61H), children baptized to Mary Robertson & Hiram Hy[de] in the Jackson/Coila church register (3:1:3Q9M-CSK3-ZSLR), 1870 residence with daughter Christina.

## Why only probable

No birth, Bible or church record of the birth has been found; all statements are secondary information from family informants.

## Parents

Not proved; see proof summary ps_002.

# Parents of Iram Hyde: not proved

**Question.** Who were the parents of Iram Hyde (born about 1796-1798, New Hampshire per q_001's probable finding; married Mary Robertson, Jackson, Washington Co., New York, c. 1820-21; died 1873, White Co., Indiana)?

**Finding.** The evidence gathered so far does not identify his parents or lean toward any candidate. The question stays open pending the death certificates and New Hampshire and probate records named below.

## Identity of the subject
Iram is identified by his 1850, 1855, 1860 and 1870 census households, the Jackson land records (mortgage 1826 and deed 1829, 'Mary his wife'; FamilySearch 3:1:3QSQ-G9WC-F61H), the Jackson/Coila church register marriage list headed 1820 ('Fran' [Iram] Hyde to Mary, FamilySearch 3:1:3Q9M-CSK3-ZSH4; primary information, but a garbled AI transcription needing image verification) and the baptism c. 1834-35 of a child to 'Mary Robertson & Hiram Hy[de]' (3:1:3Q9M-CSK3-ZSLR; primary information from the clerk). These establish him, his wife and his children, not his parents. No assertion in the church register names his parents.

## What the evidence shows
- No Hyde household appears in Jackson or its parent town Cambridge in the 1790-1820 censuses, so he arrived as an adult, consistent with a birth elsewhere (q_001: New Hampshire, probable).
- The Washington Co. Hyde households of 1810-1840 (Hampton, Hartford, Hebron, Kingsbury) are a possible kin pool, but in 1850 Iram is the only New Hampshire-born Hyde of his generation in New York, which weakens a link to them.
- New Hampshire Hyde heads of household 1790-1810 form a small candidate-father pool (Lebanon, Grafton Co.; Wolfeboro and Tamworth, Strafford Co.; Portsmouth; Lee; Colebrook; Chester). No record ties Iram to any of them. Walworth's Hyde Genealogy (1864) covers the Lebanon Hydes of the Norwich, Connecticut line and lists no Iram, which lowers that family as a candidate but does not exclude it, since Walworth may be incomplete.
- The 1880 census of daughter Margaret Clark gives her father's birthplace only; no parents' names appear in any census.

All candidates are hypotheses only and are not added to the tree. No unresolved conflict touches this question.

## Why not proved
No record located names a parent, and nothing separates the candidates. Absence from indexes and from Walworth is not a documented negative that closes the question, because named records remain unsearched.

## What could resolve it
Death certificates of daughters Christina Wilson (Indiana, 1910), Elizabeth Skellie (Pennsylvania, 1910) and Margaret Clark (Pennsylvania, 1916); New Hampshire town records for Hyde families; Washington Co. probate files naming Iram as an heir. Research-plan is where these searches would be planned.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908)

**Question:** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion:** The evidence strongly suggests that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (probable). His mother is not identified by the evidence gathered so far (not proved); a baptism record, 1880 census or the 1881 will would be the next records to examine.

### Paternity: the evidence

1. **Death certificate, 1908 (original; secondary information; direct).** Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. It names Thomas Flynn as father. The informant, son-in-law James Brown, was not present at the birth and reports what he was told, so the information is secondary. It is the only source that states the relationship outright.
2. **1850 census (original; indirect).** 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. Patrick appears in the household of Thomas Flynn (about 32, born in Ireland). The 1850 census does not state relationships, so the link is inferred from household position and shared surname; the informant is unidentified. The Ancestry index of the same census is a derivative copy and adds no independent weight.
3. **1860 census (original; indirect).** 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 15, is again in Thomas Flynn's household in the same county; relationship again inferred. Both censuses likely share the same household informant.

The two censuses show continuity of co-residence over ten years, and the death certificate, from a different informant and a different generation, independently names the same man. The two kinds of evidence agree and nothing in the gathered record contradicts them. Because the census links are inferred and the explicit statement is secondary, the finding stays at probable.

### Conflict

Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in both censuses against Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in favor of Ireland: the censuses were taken close to the birth in the household, and the certificate was given 63 years later by a son-in-law. This does not bear on identity, since name, county and Thomas Flynn as father are common to all three sources, and it does not weaken the paternity finding. The existing resolution is accepted here; note that the unextracted 1845 baptism entry at Pottsville, if it is Patrick's, would test the Ireland birthplace as well.

### Maternity

No source gathered so far names or shows a mother: the censuses as examined identify no wife in Thomas Flynn's household and the death certificate extracted here records only the father. The mother is therefore not identified by the evidence gathered so far. The 1845 St. Mary's baptism entry, the 1880 census (the first to state relationships), or Thomas Flynn's 1881 will could name her.

### Tier and limits

Paternity is probable, not proved, because (a) both censuses are indirect, (b) the one direct statement is secondary, and (c) named records that could corroborate it (will, deed, later censuses) remain unexamined. The baptism register would also narrow the maternity answer itself, which is why that claim stays not proved. Any new record could change this reading.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908)

**Question:** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion:** The evidence strongly suggests that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (probable). His mother is not identified by the evidence gathered so far. The 1845 St. Mary's baptism entry, the 1880 census or Thomas Flynn's 1881 will could name her.

### Paternity: the evidence

1. **Death certificate, 1908 (original; secondary information; direct).** Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. It names Thomas Flynn as father. The informant, son-in-law James Brown, was not present at the birth and reports what he was told, so the information is secondary. It is the only source that states the relationship outright.
2. **1850 census (original; indirect).** 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. Patrick appears in the household of Thomas Flynn (about 32, born in Ireland). The 1850 census does not state relationships, so the link is inferred from household position and shared surname, and the informant is unidentified. The Ancestry index of the same census is a derivative copy and adds no independent weight.
3. **1860 census (original; indirect).** 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 15, is again in Thomas Flynn's household in the same county, and the relationship is again inferred. Both censuses likely share the same household informant.

The censuses show co-residence over ten years. The death certificate, from a different informant and generation, independently names the same man as father. The sources agree and nothing gathered contradicts them. Because the census links are inferred and the one explicit statement is secondary, the finding stays at probable.

### Conflict

Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in both censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in favor of Ireland. The censuses were taken near the birth within the household, while the certificate was given 63 years later by a son-in-law. The dispute does not bear on identity, since name, county and Thomas Flynn as father are common to all three sources, and it does not weaken the paternity finding. The unexamined 1845 Pottsville baptism entry would also test the Ireland birthplace.

### Maternity

No source gathered so far names a mother. The death certificate extracted here records only the father, and no mother is established from the censuses as extracted. The mother is therefore not identified by the evidence gathered so far, pending the 1845 St. Mary's baptism entry, the 1880 census or Thomas Flynn's 1881 will. No mother is recorded in the tree.

### Tier and limits

Paternity is probable, not proved. Both censuses are indirect, the one direct statement is secondary, and records that could corroborate it (will, deed, later censuses) remain unexamined. Any new record could change this reading.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Parents of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

**Conclusion.** The evidence indicates that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland) of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (probable). Patrick's mother has not been identified by any record gathered so far; maternity is not proved and remains open pending the records named below.

### Evidence for paternity
No single record directly states the relationship at the time of Patrick's youth, so the case is correlated from three records.

1. **1850 census.** Patrick Flynn appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, head, in Schuylkill County: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. The source is an original; the 1850 schedule records no relationships, so the parent-child reading is inferred from household position and shared surname. The information is indeterminate and the evidence indirect. (An Ancestry index of the same schedule is a derivative copy and adds no independent weight.)
2. **1860 census.** Patrick, age 15, is again in the household of Thomas Flynn: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Original source; relationship again inferred (the census relationship column did not begin until 1880); indirect, indeterminate. Continuity of co-residence ten years later, with the age consistent, strengthens the inference but the two censuses likely share the same household informant.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of John Richardson (q_001)

**Question.** What does the Ashton-under-Lyne parish baptism register reveal about the parentage of John Richardson, the later Latter-day Saint pioneer who died 10 March 1906 at Richmond, Cache County, Utah?

**Conclusion (probable).** The evidence indicates that John Richardson was the son of Thomas Richardson, a spinner who made his mark, and Mary Mallalieu, who married at Walton-le-Dale on 12 November 1826. The parentage of the baby baptised at Ashton-under-Lyne is firmly established; the weaker link is that this baby is the Utah man, and that is why the finding is probable and not proved.

### 1. The baptism entry (direct evidence of parentage)
The original baptism register of St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, pp. 254-255, entry no. 2040, reads: "September 25 - John - Thomas X Richardson, Mary - Town - Spinner - J. Hardman" (original source; information recorded by the officiating curate in the course of duty, so primary; direct evidence of parentage; stated). Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org : accessed 22 July 2026), St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, pp. 254-255, entry no. 2040, John, son of Thomas Richardson and Mary, 25 September 1832; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm 4421674. The FamilySearch index entry (derivative, secondary, indexer as informant) agrees: father Thomas Richardson, mother Mary, 25 Sep 1832 ("England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm).

### 2. The mother's surname (indirect, correlated)
The baptism gives only "Mary". The original marriage register of St Leonard, Walton-le-Dale, p. 228, entry no. 684, records Thos Richardson (bachelor) and Mary Mallalieu (spinster) married by banns on 12 November 1826, both signing by mark, officiant Rev. Henry Fielden (original, primary, direct for the marriage; indirect for John's mother). Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm. The index entry (ark:/61903/1:1:QJDD-R1CZ) agrees. Correlation rests on the same name pair, a marriage six years before the baptism, a shared mark-signing (illiteracy) trait in both registers, and no competing Thomas and Mary pair found. The baptism-register transcription also records Mary as Mallalieu in the extraction, but the register line itself says only "Mary"; the Mallalieu surname therefore comes from the marriage correlation, not the baptism. This is common-name reasoning (Thomas and Mary Richardson in Lancashire), so it is probable, not certain.

### 3. Whether the baptised John is the Utah John (the open point)
The register gives 25 September **1832**. The project tree carried a christening date of 25 September 1833 and a birth of 24 July 1833 at Preston, none of which cites a record. A birth in July 1833 cannot precede a baptism in September 1832, so the two cannot both stand for one man. The index and the original image agree on 1832; I treat 1833 as an error in the compiled tree date. A birth about 24 July 1832 followed by baptism two months later would fit the register, but that is an inference: no source in the project states the Utah man's birth year or parents. The birthplace given in the tree (Preston) differs from the baptism place (Ashton-under-Lyne, entry marked "Town"); the parents' marriage was at Walton-le-Dale beside Preston, so a move by a mill-working family is plausible but not documented. No conflict is registered in the project for these discrepancies; they are accounted for here, and they are the reason the tier is not higher. Same name, same day and month as the tree christening, and an Ashton baptism the tree itself cites, make identity likely, but the link is by name and date only.

### 4. Tier
GPS components: research of the Lancashire registers is thorough and cites originals (components 1-3 met for the English side); identity to the Utah man rests on name, day, month and place correspondence without a Utah-side record naming his parents (component 1 gap that would narrow the answer, not only corroborate it); no registered conflict; written conclusion. Probable.

### 5. What could resolve it
A 1906 Utah death certificate, obituary, or Church record naming Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu (or giving a birthplace of Ashton-under-Lyne), the 1841 and 1851 English censuses for the household, and a Preston birth or baptism entry would test the identity link and the birth-year discrepancy. These are planned under research-plan.

The FamilySearch index entry (derivative, secondary, indexer as informant) agrees: father Thomas Richardson, mother Mary, 25 Sep 1832 ("England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm).

### 2. The mother's surname (indirect, correlated)
The baptism gives only "Mary". The original marriage register of St Leonard, Walton-le-Dale, p. 228, entry no. 684, records Thos Richardson (bachelor) and Mary Mallalieu (spinster) married by banns on 12 November 1826, both signing by mark, officiant Rev. Henry Fielden (original, primary, direct for the marriage; indirect for John's mother). Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm. The index entry (ark:/61903/1:1:QJDD-R1CZ) agrees. Correlation rests on the same name pair, a marriage six years before the baptism, a shared mark-signing (illiteracy) trait in both registers, and no competing Thomas and Mary pair found. The baptism-register transcription also records Mary as Mallalieu in the extraction, but the register line itself says only "Mary"; the Mallalieu surname therefore comes from the marriage correlation, not the baptism. This is common-name reasoning (Thomas and Mary Richardson in Lancashire), so it is probable, not certain.

### 3. Whether the baptised John is the Utah John (the open point)
The register gives 25 September **1832**. The project tree carried a christening date of 25 September 1833 and a birth of 24 July 1833 at Preston, none of which cites a record. A birth in July 1833 cannot precede a baptism in September 1832, so the two cannot both stand for one man. The index and the original image agree on 1832; I treat 1833 as an error in the compiled tree date. A birth about 24 July 1832 followed by baptism two months later would fit the register, but that is an inference: no source in the project states the Utah man's birth year or parents. The birthplace given in the tree (Preston) differs from the baptism place (Ashton-under-Lyne, entry marked "Town"); the parents' marriage was at Walton-le-Dale beside Preston, so a move by a mill-working family is plausible but not documented. No conflict is registered in the project for these discrepancies; they are accounted for here, and they are the reason the tier is not higher. Same name, same day and month as the tree christening, and an Ashton baptism the tree itself cites, make identity likely, but the link is by name and date only.

### 4. Tier
GPS components: research of the Lancashire registers is thorough and cites originals (components 1-3 met for the English side); identity to the Utah man rests on name, day, month and place correspondence without a Utah-side record naming his parents (component 1 gap that would narrow the answer, not only corroborate it); no registered conflict; written conclusion. Probable.

### 5. What could resolve it
A 1906 Utah death certificate, obituary, or Church record naming Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu (or giving a birthplace of Ashton-under-Lyne), the 1841 and 1851 English censuses for the household, and a Preston birth or baptism entry would test the identity link and the birth-year discrepancy. These are planned under research-plan.

output.text_response:
Here is the proof-conclusion agent's report:

---

**Proof Summary `ps_001` written — Question `q_001` is now resolved.**

**Tier:** Probable (shortfall: `gap`)

---

### Conclusion

Patrick Flynn's father was **very likely Thomas Flynn** of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

- Two census records ten years apart (1850 and 1860) place Patrick living in Thomas's household — indirect evidence of parentage.
- Patrick's 1908 death certificate names Thomas as his father, but the informant was a son-in-law, making that secondary information.
- No record contradicts the Thomas–Patrick relationship.
- Because no record from someone with firsthand knowledge makes the statement directly, the conclusion is **probable**, not proved.

**Maternity is not proved.** A widow named Bridget Flynn appears in 1870, but nothing ties her to Thomas or confirms she is Patrick's mother. No parent–child relationship for Bridget was written into the tree.

---

### Tree Update
A ParentChild relationship (R1) was added: Thomas Flynn (I2) → Patrick Flynn (I1), sourced to the 1850 census, 1860 census, and 1908 death certificate.

### Conflicts
c_001 (birthplace conflict) is resolved in favour of Ireland and does not bear on identity.

---

### Still Unsearched
The 1880 census, Thomas Flynn's probate file, Catholic baptism and marriage registers, and a Thomas/Bridget marriage record were not searched. A marriage or baptism record naming both parents would settle maternity.

**Next step:** The project is complete. Use the research-plan agent if you'd like to plan searches for those remaining records.

## Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. about 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Answer.** The evidence indicates that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County (probable). His mother is not identified: the one candidate, Bridget Flynn, is not established (not proved), and no maternal relationship is asserted.

### Paternity (probable)

Three sources bear on it. (1) The 1850 census lists Patrick in the household of Thomas Flynn, head (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026). (2) The 1860 census lists Patrick, age 15, again in Thomas Flynn's household (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). (3) The 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026).

Classification: both censuses are original sources, but neither states relationships before 1880, so the parent-child reading is indirect evidence inferred from household position, age and surname, with indeterminate information quality. The Ancestry 1850 index is a derivative of the same census and adds no independence. The death certificate is an original source giving direct but secondary information: the informant was James Brown, son-in-law, not present at the birth and reporting decades later. Its value is that it states the relationship explicitly, which the censuses do not. Two enumerations a decade apart placing the same boy in the same man's household, plus an explicit statement from a later family informant, point one direction and nothing contradicts them. This is a preponderance, not a proof, because no record created by someone with firsthand knowledge states the relationship.

### Conflict accounted for

Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the 1850 and 1860 censuses versus Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in favour of Ireland, because the censuses are contemporary and the son-in-law was a secondary informant. The dispute concerns birthplace, not whether the household Patrick appears in is his own. The same Patrick Flynn is tied to the three records by name, age and county, so the conflict does not undermine identity. It does flag that the death certificate informant was imperfectly informed about Patrick's origins, which is one reason the paternity is held at probable and not proved.

### Maternity (not proved)

Bridget Flynn appears as a widow aged 52 and head of her own household in the 1870 census (1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026). No record names her as Patrick's mother or as Thomas Flynn's wife, no child is enumerated with her, and Flynn is a common surname in the county. The link rests on an unsupported assumption that any Flynn widow was Thomas's, and the person-evidence link is scored 0.0002 (speculative). Maternity is therefore not established by the evidence gathered so far; it remains unresolved pending a marriage record or baptism register naming Thomas and a wife, Thomas's probate or estate file, or the 1880 census. Bridget is not written to the tree as Patrick's mother.

### Scope and limits

Research is not declared exhaustive. The 1880 census, Thomas Flynn's probate, and church baptism and marriage registers are unsearched; they would corroborate the paternal claim and could decide the maternal one. Conclusions remain open to revision with new evidence.

**Tier:** paternity probable; maternity not proved; overall probable (the stronger claim).

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Who was the mother of Cornelis van Noord, born 1828 in Zuid-Holland?

## Conclusion (possible)
The evidence indicates that Cornelis's mother was a woman recorded as "[?]annetje van Noord", who was dead by 1851 when her husband was recorded as a widower. Her given name is not settled: the evidence allows Jannetje (the OCR reading of the birth act), Fannetje (the ten-year marriage index), or Tannetje (the researcher's reading of the birth-act image). The finding is therefore a possible answer, not a firm one.

## Evidence
- **Birth act no. 42, 1828** (Burgerlijke Stand, Zuid-Holland, Netherlands, birth act no. 42, 1828, Cornelis van Noord; original record, primary information, stated by the father as informant, a household member) names the mother as "Jannetje [?] van Noord". The first letter of the given name is unclear in the handwriting; the OCR read J and the researcher reads T.
- **Ten-year marriage index 1843-1852** (Tienjarige tafels (ten-year marriage index), Zuid-Holland, Netherlands, 1843-1852, Cornelis van Noord; derivative abstract, secondary information supplied by a clerk acting in an official duty) names the mother as "Fannetje van Noord".
- The 1851 death act of Cornelis's father calls him widower of "[.]annetje van Noord", with the first letter blotted just as in the birth act. It therefore gives no independent reading, but it agrees with the other two on every letter after the first and shows the mother died before 1851.

## Conflict c_001 (unresolved)
The two sources differ only in the first letter of the given name. The birth act is the original, but its first letter cannot be read; the index is legible but is a derivative abstract of a marriage act whose own wording is not on file. The researcher's reading of the birth image is a further reading of the same entry as the OCR, not an independent witness. Neither side outweighs the other, and this conflict disputes the very fact asked (her name), so it caps the finding at possible. It does not put in doubt that all the readings describe one woman, the mother named on the birth act of Cornelis. Note also that she carries the surname van Noord, the same as the father; the project holds no record explaining this, and the clerk's recording of her surname has not been tested against a parents' marriage act.

## What was searched
Every record that could name her in full has been searched (see the search summary): the court duplicate of the 1828 register and the 1850 marriage act with its supplements do not survive, there is no death act for her or for Cornelis, no population-register entry names her, no sibling's birth exists, and no parents' marriage was found. The research has ended on this unsettled conflict.

## Tree
The tree already holds Jannetje van Noord (I2) as parent of Cornelis (I1) with no source on that edge and a single reading of the name. This conclusion does not endorse that reading over the others.
